newsitem.title: CROATIA: Angry Serbs scuffle with Croat journalists, UN.
newsitem.headline: Angry Serbs scuffle with Croat journalists, UN.

text.p: Angry Serb demonstrators on Wednesday forced a U.N. official and a group of Croatian journalists to cut short a visit to the Eastern Slavonia enclave, a United Nations spokesman said.
The incident occurred a day after Croatian president Franjo Tudjman paid an unannounced visit to the area, the last enclave under Serb control.

Eastern Slavonia broke away from Croatia after Zagreb proclaimed independence from communist Yugoslavia in 1991. The enclave, currently under U.N. administration, is due to be transferred to Croatia's control next year.

Wednesday's scuffle broke out at an exhibition of Croat and Serb children's paintings which was due to open in Vukovar, the enclave's largest town, said Philip Arnold, spokesman for the U.N.'s Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).
"Some 150-200 people were protesting against Tudjman's visit in front of the cultural centre, where the exhibition was to take place," Arnold told Reuters by telephone.
"When they saw me coming with Croatian journalists there was a scuffle, some pushing and shoving, and they prevented us from entering the building."

The demonstrators shouted abuse at Arnold, accusing him of "bringing Ustasha to Vukovar". Ustasha is the name for Croatian fascist troops, responsible for mass killings of Serbs and Jews in World War Two.
The U.N. then hurriedly put the journalists from nearby Croatian-held Osijek on a bus. "There was some banging on the doors but to my knowledge no one was hurt," Arnold said.
UNTAES's 5,000 peacekeepers are monitoring the area's gradual return to Zagreb's rule, due to be completed next year.

The process has been fraught by Serb fears of reprisals under new Croatian rule and Zagreb's hurry to reclaim lost property. Arnold said the incident did not reflect the "general mood" in the enclave.
"We are very sorry that this kind of hooliganism happened but we're happy no one was hurt."

"The people who demonstrated are the most emotional and irrational people, whose children were killed in Vukovar. They took out their anger at the only people they could and it happened to be Croatian journalists," he said.
